implementation_notes: Kotlin has no try-with-resources statement, so the standard library supplies use as an inline extension: it calls the block with the receiver and closes it in a finally equivalent, adding a close failure to the suppressed exceptions of the block's failure. What replaces the classic wrapper is that extension plus the Closeable/AutoCloseable contract; being inline, it allocates no lambda and allows non-local returns from the block. Use it as the default bracket for any Closeable resource, and drop to an explicit try/finally only when the resource is not Closeable or when several dependent resources need coordinated teardown.
code_sketch:
FileInputStream("data.bin").use { stream ->   // closed when the block exits
    process(stream)                             // body receives the resource
}

return lock.withLock { sharedState.read() }     // same shape for scoped locking
pitfalls: use is declared on a nullable receiver (T : Closeable?) and silently does nothing for null, so a failed acquisition can look like a successful no-op.
A close failure is added as a suppressed exception of the block's exception; logs that print only the top-level message lose it.
Because use is inline, a return inside the block returns from the enclosing function - convenient, but a block that was meant to be a callback can skip code the caller expected to run.

variants.name: AutoCloseable { cleanup } factory paired with use
variants.implementation_notes: Kotlin 2.0's standard library adds an AutoCloseable { cleanup } factory that wraps a cleanup action into an AutoCloseable, so no resource class is needed: build the action, hand it to use, and the cleanup runs on every exit path, including exceptions. This is the smallest realization of the pattern in the language and the modern replacement for adapting foreign resources to Closeable by hand; the trade-off against closeable-use is that the wrapped value must travel as a separate variable and the action cannot return a value, so it fits release-style cleanup rather than protocols with a result.
variants.code_sketch:
val connection = openConnection()
AutoCloseable { connection.release() }.use {   // cleanup action, no resource class
    connection.send(payload)                   // body
}
pitfalls: The factory's close action runs every time close() is invoked; make it idempotent or guard it, since use only calls it once but nothing prevents a second call.
The AutoCloseable wrapper is a different object from the resource: wrapping the same resource twice (or nesting two use blocks) double-releases it.
Because the value under management is only the wrapper, the cleanup cannot report a failure to the body; failures must be logged or thrown and will suppress the body's exception.
